summary:
MeghBhed (মেঘভেদ) finds the floods that free satellite maps miss. In July 2026, monsoon floods affected 1.28 million people around Chattogram, Bangladesh. The free C-band flood map (NASA OPERA DSWx-S1) came four days after the peak, when much of the water had drained. NASA–ISRO's NISAR L-band radar sees through monsoon cloud and passed over at the peak on 12 July. Comparing that pass with the later map, we found 169 km² of flooding the map did not show, with up to 587,000 people living within 100 m.

We built a web app with a swipe map, upazila rankings relief teams can download, flood and landslide risk layers, and a Bangla–English assistant that answers only from our results. We trained three machine-learning models (logistic regression, Random Forest, LightGBM) with 5 km spatial cross-validation. The best reached 93.3% accuracy but raised more false alarms on independent test sites, so the map uses a physics-based radar rule.

This matters because relief is planned from flood maps, and a late map sends help to the wrong places. MeghBhed shows where the water was at its peak.
details:
**What it does**

MeghBhed (মেঘভেদ, "cloud-piercer") maps floods that free satellite flood maps miss. In the July 2026 Chattogram floods, the free C-band map (NASA OPERA DSWx-S1, from Sentinel-1) was produced on 16 July, four days after the peak, when much of the water had drained. NASA–ISRO's NISAR L-band radar passed over on 12 July, near the peak, and sees through monsoon cloud. MeghBhed compares the two and shows 169 km² of open flood that the free map did not show, with up to 587,000 people living within 100 m.

**How it works**

1. Prepare the radar: NISAR L2 GCOV backscatter (HH, HV) is cropped to the district, speckle-filtered, converted to decibels and put on one 10 m grid with land cover (ESA WorldCover), terrain (Copernicus DEM, HAND), rainfall (GPM IMERG) and population (WorldPop).

2. Detect flood: a physics-based rule. A pixel is flood when its HH backscatter drops by at least 3 dB from June and falls below −14 dB on low, open ground. Water reflects radar away, so flooded fields turn dark. Permanent water is removed using four June C-band maps.

3. Compare: the NISAR flood map is compared with the 16 July C-band map on a 30 m grid. Each cell is marked as missed by the free map, seen by both, or no data. A later NISAR pass (19 July) shows how much had drained within a week (79%).

4. Benchmark machine learning: we trained logistic regression, Random Forest and LightGBM on 95,091 labelled cells using 5 km spatial cross-validation, with cut-offs tuned inside each training fold. LightGBM reached 93.3% accuracy. On independent sites based on flood reports, it marked 14% of land near places with no flood report as flooded; the radar rule marked 0.6%. We kept the rule for the map and show all four models side by side.

5. Risk maps: a Random Forest flood-risk model on open land (spatial AUC 0.88, well calibrated) and a transparent weighted landslide index for hill slopes.

**Benefits and intended impact**

• Relief teams see where the water was at the peak, not after it drained.

• Upazila rankings of affected area and people, downloadable as CSV, so the most affected are reached first.

• A Bangla–English assistant answers questions only from MeghBhed's own results, so local officers and residents can use it.

• The method is ready to run on every future NISAR pass, with the aim of a flood map within a day of each acquisition.

**Tools**

Python (NumPy, rasterio, h5py, scikit-learn, LightGBM, SHAP) in Google Colab and on team laptops for the data pipeline and model training; Vue, MapLibre GL and Vite for the web app, deployed on Vercel. Data came from free NASA Earthdata downloads (ASF DAAC, PO.DAAC, GES DISC). No special hardware was needed.

**How it is creative**

It uses NISAR, a mission whose first data arrived this year, to fix a real timing gap in disaster response. It also sets the free map and NISAR side by side on a swipe map, so anyone can see the difference in one gesture.

**Factors we considered**

• Honesty: NISAR products are provisional, people counts are labelled as upper bounds, and we report what failed. Our test for flood under tree cover did not pass its pre-set criteria, so it is not mapped.

• False alarms: a high accuracy score alone was not enough. We judged models on independent test sites.

• Fair comparison: June water and no-data areas are excluded so "missed" is never inflated.

• Language and access: Bangla and English throughout, with plain explanations of every number.
